newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds, futures head higher but remain wary of U.S.
newsitem.headline: Bunds, futures head higher but remain wary of U.S.

text.p: German Bunds started in the week in firm ground, helped higher by a more healthy-looking mark versus the dollar.

Traders said speculation over the weekend about the direction of Japanese and U.S. monetary policies, which hit the dollar but was digested relatively well by the U.S. credit markets, might have some dampening effect on Bunds, but may also lead to flows into German assets and should be supportive further out.
By 0655 GMT, the DTB June future was 15 basis points higher on the day at 101.88, having been as high as 101.90 in early trade. Analysts said the contract would try to test 102.00.
Beyond there, analysts pointed to 102.18 and 102.22 as key targets for the June contract, although they said it might encounter some difficulties before getting that far.
"The area 102.05/10 remains a strong resistance in Bunds," analysts at DMG futures and options in Frankfurt said.
In the cash market, where the 10-year benchmark Bund was offering a 5.739 percent bid yield at a price of 101.92 by 0705 GMT, traders said some curve steepening may be on the way.
With the mark gaining ground against the dollar, interest in shorter-dated paper should pick up, while international rate worries were likely to exert downward pressure up the curve.
The mark, which had tumbled to a low of 1.7389 against the dollar in late April, has staged a spirited comeback over the past few session and was trading at 1.6850 in early business on Monday.
Bunds face May cost of living and April wholesale prices data early in the week, but the pivotal news for the market will be the 1997 May tax estimates due on Thursday.

Opposition and media speculation that the estimates may show a shortfall of 20 billion marks have been played down by the government -- who say it will be around eight billion marks -- but analysts say a 15-20 billion-mark shortfall is likely.

"If (Finance Minister Theo) Waigel wants to comply with the Maastricht fiscal criteria, he will have to come up with some strong measures -- either cuts in social expenditure or a rise in taxes, both of which are highly unpopular," said Armin Kayser, German economist at Swiss Bank in Frankfurt.
Economists say that four billion marks on the deficit is roughly equivalent to 0.1 percent of gross domestic product.
For the markets, analysts said it was crucial that credible money-saving measures be announced as soon as possible. Without such a move, Bunds and the mark could be dealt a blow.
